strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem at the intersection of label noise robustness and domain generalization
Clear problem motivation with effective use of RotatedMNIST analysis and real-world examples (VLCS noise annotation)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple datasets, 11 DG/LNL baselines, and 18 combination methods
Valuable empirical insights about why naive LNL+DG combinations fail (domain distribution skewing, regularization vs. sample selection)
Simple, interpretable, and plug-and-play method that integrates easily with existing DG approaches
Good analysis of the NAG task challenges and limitations of existing methods
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: cross-domain comparisons and low-loss sample selection are intuitive extensions of existing ideas

Critical limitation inadequately discussed: method requires domain labels during training, making applicability restricted; comparison with domain-label baselines (group e) doesn't convincingly demonstrate advantage over simpler approaches

Inconsistent and marginal improvements: VLCS shows 2-3% gains, CHAMMI-CP shows mixed/negative results for some methods, synthetic noise shows high variability (6-22%) with occasional negative ID accuracy
Real-world noise validation weak: only VLCS manually annotated; synthetic noise (confusing digit pairs) may not reflect realistic corruption patterns
Theorem 1 lacks proof and is straightforward consequence of Assumption 1; Assumption 1 is strong and may not hold during early training when domain-invariant features are not yet learned
No theoretical analysis of failure modes or when noisy samples might have consistent cross-domain features
Method design choices poorly justified: vague guidance on when to apply DL4ND ('when stabilized but not overfitting'), no ablation on GMM assumption violations, GMM sensitivity analysis absent
Missing sensitivity analysis: impact of number of domains, low-loss sample ratios, distance metrics; no ablation on application timing during training
No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple runs; cannot assess reliability of marginal improvements
Reproducibility concerns: key implementation details in appendix, VLCS noise annotation criteria appear subjective, unclear hyperparameter selection process

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing an underexplored intersection of Domain Generalization and Learning with Noisy Labels, with clear illustrations of why this matters in practice
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 datasets, 11 DG methods, 4 LNL methods, and 18 combinations, with organized comparisons and thoughtful analysis
Insightful analysis of why naive LNL+DG combinations fail (Section 5.3), including useful observations about domain distribution skewing and quality vs. quantity tradeoffs
Practical and modular DL4ND approach that can be integrated as a plug-and-play preprocessing step into any DG method
Clear problem formulation with effective visualizations (Figures 1-3) demonstrating the challenge of distinguishing noise from domain shifts
Good reproducibility with detailed implementation information, algorithms, and code release promised
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: DL4ND is relatively straightforward (GMM splitting + proxy creation + cross-domain comparison) without significant algorithmic innovation

Theorem 1 and Assumption 1 lack rigor: no formal proofs, unclear conditions for validity, and no analysis of when assumptions break down. The claim that class structure dominates domain structure is strong and may not hold early in training

Critical circular dependency: the method assumes models learn clean samples first, but recent work shows this isn't guaranteed under label noise. Timing of when to apply DL4ND is dataset-dependent but not thoroughly analyzed
Modest improvements on real-world data: most improvements on true real-world datasets (VLCS, CHAMMI-CP) are <3%, and many are within noise margins without statistical significance testing
Method requires domain labels during training, a significant practical limitation not adequately discussed. Limits applicability compared to some modern DG methods
Limited real-world validation with only 2 genuinely real-world datasets, and VLCS noise annotation is subjective/manual rather than from original source
Incomplete ablation studies: no analysis of sensitivity to GMM assumptions, timing of label updates, number of domains required, or robustness to domain label noise
No statistical significance testing reported: no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs. Hard to assess if modest improvements are statistically significant
Mixed results on synthetic noise (Table 3): some methods show performance degradation (e.g., -2.5%, -0.6%), suggesting the approach isn't universally beneficial
Missing computational cost analysis and discussion of failure modes or dataset properties that affect performance

strengths: Novel problem formulation (NAG) that is practical and underexplored, combining LNL and DG in a way that mirrors real-world requirements
Clear diagnostic analysis showing why existing approaches fail, with convincing experiments on RotatedMNIST (Figure 4) demonstrating the challenge of separating noise from domain shifts
Intuitive and valuable insight that cross-domain comparisons force reliance on intrinsic rather than spurious features, well-illustrated with concrete examples
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 7 datasets, multiple noise types (synthetic and real-world), and extensive baselines (12 DG/LNL methods + 20 combinations)
Solid ablation studies (Tables 5-6) quantifying each component's contribution and demonstrating precision improvements from cross-domain comparisons
Strong commitment to reproducibility with promised code/data release and detailed implementation details
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: DL4ND primarily combines existing techniques (small-loss selection, relabeling, distance-based classification); cross-domain comparison is the main novelty but relatively straightforward

Weak theoretical foundation: Equation (2) assumes specific featurizer properties without justification; no analysis of when cross-domain comparisons are guaranteed to be more reliable; no convergence or performance guarantees

Limited real-world validation: Only 3 real-world noise datasets with mostly synthetic noise experiments; real VLCS noise is mainly unlabeled categories (Table 14), not label flips, limiting generalizability
Modest empirical improvements: Many gains are 1-2% without error bars or significance tests; Table 6 shows cross-domain precision improves only 3-10%, undermining claims of criticality

Per-domain sampling experiment (Table 7) weakens core contribution: advantage of DL4ND diminishes when domain labels separate the problem into single-domain noise detection, suggesting cross-domain comparisons mainly address problems DG creates rather than being fundamentally better

Missing critical analysis: No failure case discussion, computational cost analysis, or systematic sensitivity studies; hyperparameter tuning appears dataset-specific (Tables 12-13) suggesting potential leakage; unclear practical guidance without validation sets

Experimental concerns: Limited domain diversity (VLCS uses same-domain photo sources, CHAMMI-CP is same-lab variations); performance with 2-3 domains unexplored; some baselines perform surprisingly poorly raising implementation questions
Presentation issues: Paper is lengthy with key insights in appendices; incomplete code availability statement; some overclaimed results (e.g., 'best' when improvements are marginal <1%)
